summary:
The Ones Who Went First is an interactive web comic for school-age space fans (ages 10–14) about three NASA machines that are still out there: Surveyor 3, standing on the Moon since 1967; Pioneer 10, still drifting toward the stars, silent since 2003; and the retired Kepler telescope, still orbiting the Sun.
Each machine tells its own story in a comic, from launch to its final signal. Instead of listing facts, the comics let readers do the science: dig lunar soil with Surveyor’s scoop to test whether astronauts could land; drag a planet across a star and watch Kepler’s light curve dip; explore Jupiter’s radiation and magnetic field as Pioneer 10 did; decode the Pioneer plaque.
Every fact comes from NASA’s mission pages and is cited, and artist’s concepts and fiction are labeled. The site runs in any browser, including on phones, with no install.
Kids mostly hear about active missions. We want them to see that these silent machines made today’s exploration possible, and to feel a personal connection to them.
details:
What it does / how it works
The Ones Who Went First is a website with three interactive comics about NASA spacecraft that are still out there: Surveyor 3 on the Moon, Pioneer 10 drifting out of the solar system, and the retired Kepler telescope orbiting the Sun. On the home page, the Moon, the Sun and Jupiter are rendered live in the browser. Clicking a world flies the reader to it, where they meet the spacecraft and see a short mission card. From there they open its comic. Panels appear one at a time with the space bar or a tap, like turning pages.

The comics are told from the spacecraft’s point of view, from launch to the last signal. At key moments the reader does the science themselves:

  • tap three times to feel Surveyor 3’s real double bounce on landing;
  • drag its scoop to dig a trench and test whether the soil could hold an Apollo lander;
  • move a planet in front of a star and watch Kepler’s light curve dip (the transit method);
  • balance Kepler against sunlight to rescue it as the K2 mission;
  • fly Pioneer 10 through the asteroid belt to Jupiter, explore Jupiter’s radiation belts and magnetic field, decode the Pioneer plaque, and follow its last radio signal on its 11-hour trip to Earth.

Benefits and intended impact
School-age space fans mostly hear about active missions. Our comics show them that these “silent” machines made today’s exploration possible. Because readers interact with each discovery instead of reading a list of dates, they can understand how the mission worked and remember it. We hope readers leave with a personal connection to these robotic explorers and curiosity about the science behind them.

Tools and technologies

  • Code: HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with no frameworks. WebGL shaders render the Moon, Jupiter and the Sun procedurally. SVG is used for the interactive diagrams.
  • Hosting: GitHub Pages. Works in any modern browser, including phones, with no install.
  • SI tools: comic illustrations were generated with ChatGPT and carry a visible “SI-generated” watermark. Code and English captions were written with the help of Claude (Anthropic) and checked against NASA sources. All SI use is listed in the README and on the site.
  • Data: NASA mission pages for Surveyor 3, Pioneer 10 and Kepler (the Space Apps resources), plus NASA news releases for extra details.

Creativity
Instead of a fact page, each spacecraft narrates its own story in a comic. The interactions are the actual science, not decoration. The Pioneer 10 comic ends with a clearly labeled imagined epilogue: someone, someday, finds the plaque.

Factors we considered

  • Accuracy: every fact was checked against NASA sources. Schematic diagrams, the artist’s concept of Kepler-186f and the fictional epilogue are labeled as such.
  • Age: about 10–14, with short captions.
  • Accessibility: keyboard and touch controls, a mobile layout, and support for reduced motion.
dataRefs: NASA news release, “NASA’s Kepler Telescope Discovers First Earth-Size Planet in ‘Habitable Zone’”. Used for Kepler-186f: its 130-day orbit, the one-third of Earth’s energy it receives, its ~500 light-year distance and its location in Cygnus.
NASA, Kepler-186f page with the July 2015 update on Kepler-452b
NASA Science, article on Kepler’s reaction wheel failures (the first in July 2012, the second in May 2013)
projectRefs: The Planetary Society, “The Pioneer Plaque: Science as a Universal Language”. Used for the hydrogen symbol and the 21 cm unit.
Space.com, for Kepler’s reaction wheel numbering (wheels 2 and 4)
